now.v: Synapse, a local-first memory for agents. It only cares about two numbers: speed and cost.
Synapse against LongMemEval. Vibes are not a metric.
Lunch & learns at work on Claude: memory, artifacts, video. The goal is for the whole company to show up.
Weird web behavior, for a talk. I’d rather build a tiny broken version than read another tutorial.

chapters.b: The first thing people actually used was a Go tool that pulls 20,000+ V2Ray configs, dedupes them and rebuilds the list every 6 hours. A run takes 11 seconds. It has 155 stars now, which is wild. That’s when speed became my whole personality.

Next I got into networks that don’t want to be mapped. I wrote a scanner that pokes Cloudflare and Fastly edges and flags DPI tricks and MITM, then built a live dashboard that tracks internet shutdowns in Iran. Some code matters more than the rest.
December 2025: I graduated from Computer Programming at Algonquin College. My curiosity didn’t. It got worse.
Then I noticed AI agents forget everything, and it felt like a bug in the universe. Now most of my days go to memory systems, local-first stuff and open source. No regrets. Mostly.

loves.b: Your data. Your disk. If it needs someone else’s server to remember your name, you’re renting it.
No benchmark? Then it’s a guess. I learned that the hard way, and it’s in my writing.
Runtimes, compilers, networking, databases, Unicode and RTL text. The “wait, why does it do that?” stuff.
Reading other people’s code is the fastest way to get humbled. I love it.

projects.name: synapse
projects.story: Chat history is a log. Synapse is a brain. It's a local-first memory for AI agents, all on SQLite. It pulls facts out of conversations and pins single-value facts to keys like user.employer, so a new job overwrites the old one instead of both being "true". Retrieval mixes FTS5/BM25 with vector search, no LLM by default, and every hit carries a trust note like "stored 8 months ago, may be outdated". Oh, and it refuses to store anything that looks like a credential.

projects.name: v2go
projects.story: Public V2Ray subscription lists are mostly dead servers. A port check doesn't tell you much either: something answering on 443 says nothing about whether the proxy works. So v2go runs every config through an embedded Xray-core and sends a real request through it. Every hour it grabs about 50,000 configs, dedupes them down to 10–15k, live-tests them all in about two minutes and publishes the few hundred that actually carried traffic. No subprocesses, no open ports.

projects.name: cf-knife
projects.story: A pocket knife for networks that hate being mapped. It scans Cloudflare and Fastly ranges in layers (TCP, TLS, HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, HTTP/3) and has nmap-style timing templates, from paranoid to insane. Then it gets nosy. It fragments TLS ClientHellos to test DPI, compares your resolver against DoH to catch DNS poisoning, and checks certificate chains for MITM. It's one static binary, and the scan state lives in SQLite, so you can resume.

projects.name: iran-internet-monitor
projects.story: When the internet goes dark, somebody should be counting. Every 10 minutes, one Go binary probes 40 endpoints and about 1,070 Iranian IP ranges from outside Iran, and an LLM analyst reads the results. Per-operator data is what separates an ISP outage from a national shutdown. Every pass is a git commit, so the whole history is open data. The probes are honest about where they run: if a fake address "connects", something is intercepting traffic and the sweep gets thrown out instead of published.

projects.name: llm-map
projects.story: Every AI language model on one 3D chart. Each dot is a model, each line is one company's models from oldest to newest, and you pick the three axes: smartness, cost, speed, price, ARC-AGI-2 or release date. One switch lights up the models nothing else beats on all three. You can drag a little figure onto a line and ride through a company's history. It runs on a Cloudflare Worker that merges Artificial Analysis and ARC Prize data. It's a PWA, and it speaks Persian, right to left, with the Solar Hijri calendar.

projects.name: syncodoro
projects.story: A Pomodoro timer that doesn't care if you're offline. Sessions go into IndexedDB first and sync to Supabase when you're back. You can tag and annotate sessions, export them as CSV or ICS straight into your calendar, and look at stats that show how locked in you really were. Usually less than you think.

projects.name: free-macos
projects.story: macOS never shipped Linux's free command, so I wrote one. It's live in your terminal, with progress bars for used, free, active, wired and compressed memory. Alias it to free and forget it was ever missing.

projects.name: netray
projects.story: A scanner for Cloudflare VLESS/VMess configs. Feed it a file or a subscription URL and it measures TCP and TLS handshake latency per IP, then exports the best ones ranked. The Clean IP Finder goes from a 30-second scan of about 4K IPs up to all ~1.5M Cloudflare IPv4 addresses on two ports. Interactive TUI or headless, your pick.

experience.b: Memory tools that agents check before every answer, even when they’d rather not.

title: boo. i’m dani.
i give ai agents a memory.
body: Every AI agent you’ve used forgets you the second the tab closes. Every. Single. One.
That bugs me way more than it should. So I’m building them a memory that lives on your laptop, not in a data center. Open source, local-first, and still a little broken. Getting there.
